claims.claim: God commands a freewill offering of gold, silver, brass, blue, purple, scarlet, fine linen, goats' hair, rams' skins dyed red, badgers' skins, shittim wood, oil, spices, and onyx stones, taken "of every man that giveth it willingly with his heart" (25:1–7).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 25:1–7, read in full.

claims.claim: The sanctuary's stated purpose is God's dwelling: "let them make me a sanctuary; that I may dwell among them" (25:8).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 25:8, read in full.

claims.claim: Everything is to be made "according to all that I shew thee, after the pattern of the tabernacle, and the pattern of all the instruments thereof" (25:9) — a revealed pattern, shown on the mount.
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 25:9, read in full; Philo Vit. Mos. II.74 ("incorporeal patterns… contemplated with his soul").

claims.claim: The ark is of shittim wood, 2½ × 1½ × 1½ cubits, overlaid with pure gold within and without, with a crown of gold, four gold rings, and gold-overlaid staves that "shall not be taken from it"; the testimony is put inside (25:10–16).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 25:10–16, read in full; Josephus Ant. 3.134–138.

claims.claim: The mercy seat is of pure gold, 2½ × 1½ cubits, with two cherubim of beaten work at its ends, wings stretched out, faces toward each other and toward the mercy seat; "there I will meet with thee, and I will commune with thee from above the mercy seat, from between the two cherubims" (25:17–22).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 25:17–22, read in full; BDB H3727 (kappōret, "propitiatory"; the cherubim's wings "constituted the throne of Yahweh").

claims.claim: The table is of shittim wood, 2 × 1 × 1½ cubits, overlaid with pure gold, with crown, border, rings, staves, and vessels of pure gold; "thou shalt set upon the table shewbread before me alway" (25:23–30).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 25:23–30, read in full; Josephus Ant. 3.139–143 (twelve loaves, replaced every Sabbath).

claims.claim: The lampstand is of pure gold, one beaten work, with shaft, six branches, almond-shaped bowls, knops, and flowers, and seven lamps that "give light over against it"; it is made "of a talent of pure gold," "after their pattern, which was shewed thee in the mount" (25:31–40).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 25:31–40, read in full; Josephus Ant. 3.144–146 (100 pounds; seven branches "in imitation of the number of the planets").

claims.claim: The tabernacle has ten curtains of fine twined linen, blue, purple, and scarlet, with cherubim, 28 × 4 cubits, coupled with fifty loops and fifty gold taches; eleven goat-hair curtains, 30 × 4 cubits, with brass taches; a covering of rams' skins dyed red and a covering above of badgers' skins (26:1–14).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 26:1–14, read in full; Josephus Ant. 3.130–133.

claims.claim: The identity of taḥaš (H8476, KJV "badgers' skins," 25:5; 26:14) is uncertain: BDB defines it as "a kind of leather or skin, and perhaps the animal yielding it (probably the dugong…)"; ISBE judges the KJV rendering "indeed incorrect" (RV "sealskins," margin "porpoise skins"). No modern identification is established.
claims.evidence: BDB H8476 and ISBE, read via BibleHub.

claims.claim: The boards are of shittim wood standing up, 10 × 1½ cubits, two tenons each: twenty south, twenty north, six west plus two corner boards, on silver sockets (two per board), overlaid with gold, with five gold-overlaid bars each side and a middle bar reaching end to end; the tabernacle is reared "according to the fashion thereof which was shewed thee in the mount" (26:15–30).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 26:15–30, read in full; Josephus Ant. 3.116–121.

claims.claim: The veil of blue, purple, scarlet, and fine linen with cherubim hangs on four gold-overlaid pillars on silver sockets and divides "between the holy place and the most holy"; the mercy seat is put on the ark in the most holy; the table stands on the north side and the lampstand on the south; the door hanging is on five pillars with brass sockets (26:31–37).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 26:31–37, read in full; Josephus Ant. 3.122–129.

claims.claim: The altar of burnt offering is of shittim wood, 5 × 5 × 3 cubits, foursquare, with horns of the same, overlaid with brass, with pans, shovels, basons, fleshhooks, firepans, a grate of network, and staves; it is "hollow with boards… as it was shewed thee in the mount" (27:1–8).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 27:1–8, read in full; Josephus Ant. 3.149.

claims.claim: The court is 100 × 50 cubits of fine twined linen hangings, five cubits high, on twenty brass-socketed pillars south and north and ten west, with a twenty-cubit gate of blue, purple, scarlet, and linen on four pillars; all the vessels and pins of the tabernacle and court are brass (27:9–19).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 27:9–19, read in full; Josephus Ant. 3.108–114.

claims.claim: Pure olive oil beaten is brought "to cause the lamp to burn always"; Aaron and his sons order it from evening to morning before the LORD, "a statute for ever unto their generations" (27:20–21).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 27:20–21, read in full.

claims.claim: The tabernacle is organised in three graded zones — outer court, holy place, most holy place — with access restricted at each boundary (veil, 26:33; cf. Lev 16:2).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 26:33; 27:9–19, read in full.

claims.claim: The text gives every dimension in cubits and nowhere defines the cubit's length; any metric or imperial equivalent is a conventional estimate, not the text's statement.
claims.evidence: Absence verified by reading Ex 25–27 in full.

claims.claim: The ark is the only object placed in the most holy place, and the mercy seat is its cover, not a separate vessel (25:21–22; 26:34).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 25:21–22; 26:34, read in full.

claims.claim: The lampstand stands on the south side of the tabernacle, over against the table on the north, and its seven lamps give light "over against it" (25:37; 26:35).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 25:37; 26:35, read in full; Philo Vit. Mos. II.102 (south side, figuring the stars).

claims.claim: Aaron and his sons Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar, and Ithamar are taken from among Israel "that he may minister unto me in the priest's office" (28:1).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 28:1, read in full.

claims.claim: The holy garments are made "for glory and for beauty" (28:2) by all "that are wise hearted, whom I have filled with the spirit of wisdom" (28:3).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 28:2–3, read in full.

claims.claim: The garments are six: breastplate, ephod, robe, broidered coat, mitre, and girdle, of gold, blue, purple, scarlet, and fine twined linen (28:4–5).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 28:4–5, read in full.

claims.claim: The ephod is of gold, blue, purple, scarlet, and fine linen, with two shoulderpieces and a curious girdle; two onyx stones engraved with the names of Israel, six on each stone "according to their birth," are set in gold ouches on the shoulders "for stones of memorial," and "Aaron shall bear their names before the LORD upon his two shoulders for a memorial" (28:6–14).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 28:6–14, read in full.

claims.claim: The breastplate of judgment is foursquare, doubled, a span square, of the ephod's materials, with four rows of stones — sardius, topaz, carbuncle; emerald, sapphire, diamond; ligure, agate, amethyst; beryl, onyx, jasper — twelve stones "with the names of the children of Israel… according to the twelve tribes" (28:15–21).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 28:15–21, read in full.

claims.claim: The modern mineral identity of several of the twelve stones is uncertain; the KJV names (e.g., "ligure," "carbuncle") are traditional renderings, and modern identifications differ.
claims.evidence: The KJV list is established (clm-ta-023); the identifications are disputed in the literature and no gemmological source was consulted in this session.

claims.claim: "Aaron shall bear the names of the children of Israel in the breastplate of judgment upon his heart, when he goeth in unto the holy place, for a memorial before the LORD continually," and "thou shalt put in the breastplate of judgment the Urim and the Thummim; and they shall be upon Aaron's heart… and Aaron shall bear the judgment of the children of Israel upon his heart before the LORD continually" (28:29–30).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 28:29–30, read in full.

claims.claim: The text never explains what the Urim and the Thummim were or how they functioned; their nature and mechanism are not stated anywhere in Exodus 25–34.
claims.evidence: Absence verified by reading Ex 28 in full; no source read in this session explains them from the text.

claims.claim: The robe of the ephod is all blue, with pomegranates of blue, purple, and scarlet and bells of gold alternating around its hem, "and it shall be upon Aaron to minister: and his sound shall be heard when he goeth in unto the holy place before the LORD, and when he cometh out, that he die not" (28:31–35).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 28:31–35, read in full.

claims.claim: A plate of pure gold engraved "HOLINESS TO THE LORD" is put on a blue lace upon the forefront of the mitre, "that Aaron may bear the iniquity of the holy things, which the children of Israel shall hallow in all their holy gifts" (28:36–38).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 28:36–38, read in full.

claims.claim: The embroidered linen coat, linen mitre, and needlework girdle are for Aaron; coats, girdles, and bonnets are made for his sons "for glory and for beauty"; linen breeches cover their nakedness; all is "a statute for ever unto him and his seed after him" (28:39–43).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 28:39–43, read in full.

claims.claim: The consecration takes one young bullock and two rams without blemish, unleavened bread, cakes, and wafers; Aaron and his sons are washed, vested, and anointed with oil poured on the head; the priest's office is theirs "for a perpetual statute" (29:1–9).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 29:1–9, read in full.

claims.claim: The blood rites: the bullock's blood is put on the horns of the altar; the ram's blood is put "upon the tip of the right ear of Aaron, and upon the tip of the right ear of his sons, and upon the thumb of their right hand, and upon the great toe of their right foot"; blood and anointing oil are sprinkled on Aaron, his sons, and their garments (29:10–21).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 29:10–21, read in full.

claims.claim: The ram of consecration's fat, rump, and right shoulder, with a loaf, a cake, and a wafer, are waved as a wave offering and burnt; the breast of the wave offering and the shoulder of the heave offering are Aaron's and his sons' "by a statute for ever"; the holy garments pass to Aaron's sons after him (29:22–28).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 29:22–28, read in full.

claims.claim: The consecration lasts seven days; every day a bullock is offered for a sin offering for atonement and the altar is cleansed and anointed; "seven days thou shalt make an atonement for the altar, and sanctify it; and it shall be an altar most holy: whatsoever toucheth the altar shall be holy" (29:35–37).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 29:35–37, read in full.

claims.claim: The continual burnt offering is two lambs of the first year day by day, one in the morning and one at even, with flour, oil, and wine; "there I will meet with you, to speak there unto thee… And I will dwell among the children of Israel, and will be their God" (29:38–46).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 29:38–46, read in full.

claims.claim: The altar of incense is of shittim wood, 1 × 1 × 2 cubits, overlaid with pure gold, with a crown and rings; Aaron burns sweet incense on it every morning and evening, "a perpetual incense before the LORD"; no strange incense, burnt sacrifice, or drink offering is offered on it; Aaron makes atonement on its horns once a year, and "it is most holy unto the LORD" (30:1–10).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 30:1–10, read in full; Josephus Ant. 3.147–148.

claims.claim: At the census every man twenty years old and above gives half a shekel "after the shekel of the sanctuary (a shekel is twenty gerahs)" as "a ransom for his soul unto the LORD… that there be no plague among them"; rich and poor give the same; the money is appointed "for the service of the tabernacle of the congregation… a memorial" (30:11–16).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 30:11–16, read in full.

claims.claim: The laver of brass stands between the tabernacle and the altar; Aaron and his sons wash their hands and feet there when they go in or come near to minister, "that they die not: and it shall be a statute for ever to them" (30:17–21).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 30:17–21, read in full; Josephus Ant. 3.114.

claims.claim: The holy anointing oil is compounded of pure myrrh 500 shekels, sweet cinnamon 250, sweet calamus 250, cassia 500, and olive oil one hin; it anoints the tabernacle, ark, table, lampstand, altars, laver, Aaron, and his sons; it is not poured on man's flesh and no like composition may be made, on pain of being cut off (30:22–33).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 30:22–33, read in full.

claims.claim: The incense is compounded of stacte, onycha, galbanum, and pure frankincense in equal weight, "tempered together, pure and holy," beaten small and put before the testimony; it is not made for personal use, on pain of being cut off (30:34–38).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 30:34–38, read in full.

claims.claim: Bezalel son of Uri, son of Hur, of the tribe of Judah, is called by name and "filled… with the spirit of God, in wisdom, and in understanding, and in knowledge, and in all manner of workmanship"; Aholiab son of Ahisamach of Dan is given with him, and wisdom is put "in the hearts of all that are wise hearted" to make all that is commanded (31:1–11). Josephus adds that Bezalel was the grandson of Miriam (Ant. 3.105) — his addition, not in Exodus.
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 31:1–11, read in full; Josephus Ant. 3.104–107.

claims.claim: "When the people saw that Moses delayed to come down out of the mount, the people gathered themselves together unto Aaron, and said unto him, Up, make us gods, which shall go before us; for as for this Moses, the man that brought us up out of the land of Egypt, we wot not what is become of him" (32:1).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 32:1, read in full; NETS 32:1 ("make us gods who will go before us").

claims.claim: The text states no motive for Aaron's demand for the gold earrings (32:2) or for the people's compliance (32:3). K&D reads the demand as craftiness meant to divert the people; Calvin reads unmitigated impiety. Both are interpretations; neither is the text's statement.
claims.evidence: K&D Ex 32:2–3; Calvin, Harmony of the Law III, Ex 32:1.

claims.claim: Aaron "received them at their hand, and fashioned it with a graving tool, after he had made it a molten calf" (32:4). K&D argues the calf was first formed of wood and then covered with gold plate (massēkâ as gold coating, Isa 40:19; 30:22), a reconstruction supported by the destruction in 32:20 (burnt, then ground; cf. Deut 9:21).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 32:4; K&D Ex 32:4, 20; Deut 9:21.

claims.claim: ʿēgel (H5695) is a young bull (BDB; K&D). Its form copies the Egyptian bull: K&D (following Hengstenberg) says it was "copied from the Egyptian Apis"; JFB calls Apis "the chief deity of the Egyptians, worshipped at Memphis under the form of a live ox"; Philo says it was made "in imitation of that which appeared to be the most sacred animal in that district" (Vit. Mos. II.162). Hathor's Sinai shrines (§4.2) make a bovine goddess a live alternative to Apis.
claims.evidence: BDB H5695; K&D Ex 32:4; JFB Ex 32; Philo Vit. Mos. II.162; §4.2.

claims.claim: The calf is presented as an image of YHWH, not of a foreign god: "These be thy gods, O Israel, which brought thee up out of the land of Egypt" (32:4), and Aaron proclaims "To morrow is a feast to the LORD" (32:5). K&D, JFB, and Bible Odyssey agree; Ps 106:19–20 adopts the same reading.
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 32:4–5; K&D Ex 32:4–6; JFB Ex 32; Bible Odyssey, "The Worship of the Golden Calf"; Ps 106:19–20.

claims.claim: The people "rose up early on the morrow, and offered burnt offerings, and brought peace offerings; and the people sat down to eat and to drink, and rose up to play" (32:6). K&D reads the "play" (ṣāḥaq) as sacrificial meals, sports, antiphonal songs, and dances "in the same manner in which the Egyptians celebrated their feast of Apis (Herod. 2.60, and 3.27)."
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 32:6; K&D Ex 32:5–6 (Herodotus cited through K&D).

claims.claim: God tells Moses on the mountain: "thy people, which thou broughtest out of the land of Egypt, have corrupted themselves: they have turned aside quickly out of the way which I commanded them: they have made them a molten calf, and have worshipped it, and have sacrificed thereunto" (32:7–8).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 32:7–8, read in full.

claims.claim: "I have seen this people, and, behold, it is a stiffnecked people: now therefore let me alone, that my wrath may wax hot against them, and that I may consume them: and I will make of thee a great nation" (32:9–10).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 32:9–10, read in full. (The LXX omits MT 32:9 — see §3.2.)

claims.claim: Moses intercedes with three appeals: God's own acts toward Israel (32:11), his honour in the sight of the Egyptians (32:12), and the promises sworn to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob (32:13).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 32:11–13, read in full.

claims.claim: "And the LORD repented of the evil which he thought to do unto his people" (32:14).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 32:14, read in full; NETS 32:14 ("the Lord was propitiated concerning the harm"). The theological reading (anthropopathic) is traditional interpretation — see §8.5.

claims.claim: Moses descends with "the two tables of the testimony… written on both their sides; on the one side and on the other were they written. And the tables were the work of God, and the writing was the writing of God, graven upon the tables" (32:15–16).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 32:15–16, read in full.

claims.claim: Joshua hears the noise and says, "There is a noise of war in the camp"; Moses answers, "It is not the voice of them that shout for mastery, neither is it the voice of them that cry for being overcome; but the noise of them that sing do I hear" (32:17–18). K&D reads "the sound of antiphonal songs" (cf. Ex 15:21).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 32:17–18, read in full; K&D Ex 32:15–18.

claims.claim: "As soon as he came nigh unto the camp, that he saw the calf, and the dancing: and Moses' anger waxed hot, and he cast the tables out of his hands, and brake them beneath the mount" (32:19).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 32:19, read in full. K&D reads the breaking as "a sign that Israel had broken the covenant" (§8).

claims.claim: Moses "took the calf which they had made, and burnt it in the fire, and ground it to powder, and strawed it upon the water, and made the children of Israel drink of it" (32:20). K&D explains the sequence by the wooden core (burnt to charcoal) and the gold coating (ground to powder; Deut 9:21), and reads the drinking as a visible sign of sin and its consequences, as the suspected adulteress drinks the curse-water (Num 5:24).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 32:20; K&D Ex 32:20; Deut 9:21.

claims.claim: Aaron's excuse: "thou knowest the people, that they are set on mischief… I cast it into the fire, and there came out this calf" (32:22–24). Moses asks, "What did this people unto thee, that thou hast brought so great a sin upon them?" (32:21).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 32:21–24, read in full.

claims.claim: "When Moses saw that the people were naked; (for Aaron had made them naked unto their shame among their enemies:) then Moses stood in the gate of the camp, and said, Who is on the LORD's side? let him come unto me. And all the sons of Levi gathered themselves together unto him" (32:25–26).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 32:25–26, read in full; Philo Vit. Mos. II.167–170.

claims.claim: The Levites, commanded to go "from gate to gate throughout the camp, and slay every man his brother, and every man his companion, and every man his neighbour," kill "about three thousand men" that day (32:27–28).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 32:27–28, read in full; Philo Vit. Mos. II.171–172.

claims.claim: The severity is defended by K&D (covenant breach as a capital crime; separation of penitent from stiff-necked; Calvin's decimation parallel — "out of six hundred thousand only three thousand were put to death") and is treated as a problem by modern readers. The text gives no justification.
claims.evidence: K&D Ex 32:27–29; Calvin via K&D.

claims.claim: "For Moses had said, Consecrate yourselves to day to the LORD, even every man upon his son, and upon his brother; that he may bestow upon you a blessing this day" (32:29). K&D reads "fill your hand" as consecration (a gift for the LORD; cf. Deut 33:9); Jonathan/Kurtz read it as expiatory sacrifice for the blood shed.
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 32:29; K&D Ex 32:29.

claims.claim: Moses says to the people, "Ye have sinned a great sin: and now I will go up unto the LORD; peradventure I shall make an atonement for your sin" (32:30), and to God, "if thou wilt forgive their sin—; and if not, blot me, I pray thee, out of thy book which thou hast written" (32:31–32). K&D identifies the book as the book of life (Ps 69:29; Dan 12:1).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 32:30–32, read in full; K&D Ex 32:30–34.

claims.claim: God answers, "Whosoever hath sinned against me, him will I blot out of my book. Therefore now go, lead the people unto the place of which I have spoken unto thee: behold, mine Angel shall go before thee: nevertheless in the day when I visit I will visit their sin upon them" (32:33–34).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 32:33–34, read in full.

claims.claim: "And the LORD plagued the people, because they made the calf, which Aaron made" (32:35). The nature of the plague is not specified; K&D/Calvin (via the biblia.work aggregation) read it as sufferings of various kinds, not necessarily pestilence.
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 32:35, read in full; K&D Ex 32:35; Calvin via biblia.work.

claims.claim: Both Josephus (Ant. 3.75–101) and Augustine (City of God XVI.43) retell the giving of the law, the forty days, and the tabernacle's dedication without any mention of the golden calf. The omission is verified by direct reading of both passages.
claims.evidence: Josephus Ant. 3.75–101 (Lexundria, Whiston); Augustine CD XVI.43 (Dods, Logic Museum).

claims.claim: Josephus gives no reason for omitting the calf; any motive (e.g., apologetic suppression for a Gentile readership) is inference, not his statement.
claims.evidence: Ant. 3.75–101 read in full; no motive stated in the text.

claims.claim: Philo retells the calf after the tabernacle's furnishing and the priests' consecration (Vit. Mos. II.159–173), reordering the Exodus sequence, and makes Levi's zeal the origin of the priesthood: "it was fitting that those who had undertaken a voluntary war for the sake of the honour of God… should be thought worthy to receive the priesthood" (§173).
claims.evidence: Philo Vit. Mos. II.159–173 (Yonge, CCEL).

claims.claim: God orders the departure to the land sworn to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, promises to send an angel and drive out the nations, but says, "I will not go up in the midst of thee; for thou art a stiffnecked people: lest I consume thee in the way" (33:1–3).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 33:1–3, read in full.

claims.claim: "When the people heard these evil tidings, they mourned: and no man did put on him his ornaments. And the children of Israel stripped themselves of their ornaments by the mount Horeb" (33:4–6).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 33:4–6, read in full; NETS 33:6 ("from the mountain of Choreb").

claims.claim: "Moses took the tabernacle, and pitched it without the camp, afar off from the camp, and called it the Tabernacle of the congregation. And it came to pass, that every one which sought the LORD went out unto the tabernacle of the congregation, which was without the camp." When Moses enters, the cloudy pillar descends and stands at the door; "the LORD spake unto Moses face to face, as a man speaketh unto his friend"; Joshua "departed not out of the tabernacle" (33:7–11).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 33:7–11, read in full; NETS 33:7 ("tent of witness").

claims.claim: The tent of Ex 33:7–11 is Moses' own tent pitched outside the camp; it is distinct from the tabernacle of Ex 25–26, which has been instructed but not yet built (construction is Ex 35–40, Category 7).
claims.evidence: Canonical order Ex 25–26 (instructions) vs. Ex 33:7 (a tent already pitched) vs. Ex 35–40 (construction).

claims.claim: Moses pleads: "thou hast not let me know whom thou wilt send with me… shew me now thy way, that I may know thee… consider that this nation is thy people"; "If thy presence go not with me, carry us not up hence"; God answers, "My presence shall go with thee, and I will give thee rest" (33:12–17).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 33:12–17, read in full.

claims.claim: "I beseech thee, shew me thy glory." God answers, "I will make all my goodness pass before thee, and I will proclaim the name of the LORD before thee; and will be gracious to whom I will be gracious, and will shew mercy on whom I will shew mercy… Thou canst not see my face: for there shall no man see me, and live… I will put thee in a clift of the rock, and will cover thee with my hand while I pass by: and I will take away mine hand, and thou shalt see my back parts: but my face shall not be seen" (33:18–23).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 33:18–23, read in full (BibleGateway search text).

claims.claim: "Hew thee two tables of stone like unto the first: and I will write upon these tables the words that were in the first tables, which thou brakest"; no man or beast is to come up the mount (34:1–3).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 34:1–3, read in full (BibleGateway search text).

claims.claim: "The LORD descended in the cloud, and stood with him there, and proclaimed the name of the LORD. And the LORD passed by before him, and proclaimed, The LORD, The LORD God, merciful and gracious, longsuffering, and abundant in goodness and truth, keeping mercy for thousands, forgiving iniquity and transgression and sin, and that will by no means clear the guilty; visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children, and upon the children's children, unto the third and to the fourth generation" (34:5–7). Moses bows, worships, and pleads, "let my Lord, I pray thee, go among us; for it is a stiffnecked people; and pardon our iniquity and our sin, and take us for thine inheritance" (34:9).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 34:5–7, 9, read in full (vv. 5–6 via BibleGateway search text; vv. 9–35 read in the earlier session).

claims.claim: The covenant is renewed: "Behold, I make a covenant: before all thy people I will do marvels"; the prohibitions follow (no covenant with the land's inhabitants, destroy their altars, no molten gods, the feasts, the firstborn, the Sabbath, the firstfruits); Moses is on the mount forty days and forty nights without bread or water, and "he wrote upon the tables the words of the covenant, the ten commandments" (34:10–28).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 34:10–28, read in full (earlier session).

claims.claim: Moses descends with the two tables and "wist not that the skin of his face shone while he talked with him"; Aaron and Israel fear to come near; Moses puts a veil on his face when he has finished speaking to them and takes it off when he goes in to speak with the LORD (34:29–35).
claims.evidence: KJV Ex 34:29–35, read in full (earlier session). The veil's purpose is not stated — see §8.8.

claims.claim: The early-date position: 1 Kgs 6:1 (480 years; Solomon's fourth year c. 966 BC) puts the exodus c. 1446 BC, in the Eighteenth Dynasty, with Thutmose III as the king of the oppression and Amenhotep II as the pharaoh of the exodus; Jephthah's 300 years (Judg 11:26) and the Amarna Habiru are cited in support. The position and its evidence are as stated; the date itself is unresolved.
claims.evidence: BiblicalTraining, "Exodus" (date section); Vannoy, Session 1B.

claims.claim: The late-date position: Ex 1:11 (the store city Rameses) and Pi-Ramesses, built by Ramesses II (c. 1279–1213 BC), place the exodus c. 1270–1260 BC; the 480 years of 1 Kgs 6:1 is read as twelve generations of forty years, a schematic total. The position and its evidence are as stated; the date itself is unresolved.
claims.evidence: BiblicalTraining, "Exodus" (date section); Vannoy, Session 1B.

claims.claim: The Merneptah Stele (fifth regnal year, c. 1208 BCE) contains the earliest widely accepted extra-biblical reference to Israel — "Israel is laid waste; its seed is no more" — with the determinative for a people, not a land; it is a terminus ante quem for the exodus. It says nothing about Moses, slavery, or an exodus.
claims.evidence: BiblicalTraining; Judkins, "The Archaeology of Egypt, Part 7"; echoesofhistorypast (secondary summaries); stele text verified via the Biblical Archaeology article read in full — source-merneptah-stele (PA's verified entry; V2 fix, verification-all7-20261118.md).

claims.claim: The location of Mount Sinai is unknown. Jebel Musa (2,285 m) is traditional since the 4th century CE; alternatives include Jebel Serbal, Gabal Sin Bishar (Har-El 1983), Jebel Helal, Har Karkom (Anati), Hala-'l Badr (Musil; Humphreys), and Jebel al-Lawz (popular, rejected by archaeologists). Hoffmeier: "no one today can be certain of its location"; Kitchen: "certainty is not attainable." No Exodus-related remains have been recovered in the Sinai Peninsula.
claims.evidence: Torah Atlas, "Mount Sinai"; Patheos/Armstrong (Hoffmeier, Kitchen); israelspot/BAS (Shanks). The archaeological negative is reported second-hand and is probable, not established.

claims.claim: Jubilees 1 dates the exodus to 2450 Anno Mundi (1:1, third month, sixteenth day) and has God promise, "I will build My sanctuary in their midst, and I will dwell with them" (1:16–17), commanding, "Write for Moses from the beginning of creation till My sanctuary has been built among them for all eternity" (1:26); the angel of the presence takes the heavenly tablets (1:28–29). The 2450 A.M. date is Jubilees' own chronology.
claims.evidence: Jubilees ch. 1 (Charles, CCEL), read in full.

claims.claim: Augustine counts 144 years from Joseph's death to the exodus (City of God XVI.43), against the 430 years of Ex 12:40; he also places the giving of the law on the fiftieth day after the Passover (Ex 19:1 says only "the third month"). Both are Augustine's computations, not the biblical text's.
claims.evidence: Augustine CD XVI.43 (Dods, Logic Museum); KJV Ex 12:40; 19:1.

claims.claim: Josephus and Philo read the tabernacle as an image of the cosmos: Josephus (Ant. 3.123) — the holy of holies is "a heaven peculiar to God" and the twenty cubits "sea and land"; Philo (Vit. Mos. II.88–89, 102) — the materials are the four elements and the lampstand figures the stars; Josephus (Ant. 3.146) — the seven branches imitate "the number of the planets." This is their interpretation, received in the tradition; Exodus never says the tabernacle symbolises the cosmos.
claims.evidence: Josephus Ant. 3.123, 146; Philo Vit. Mos. II.88–89, 102.

claims.claim: The New Testament receives this category's material: the tabernacle as copy and shadow and Christ as high priest of the true tabernacle (Heb 8:5; 9:1–12, 24); "the Word became flesh, and dwelt [tabernacled] among us" (John 1:14); "the tabernacle of God is with men" (Rev 21:3); the calf as a warning against idolatry (1 Cor 10:7, quoting "the people sat down to eat and drink, and rose up to play"); Stephen's charge that Israel "made a calf" and God "gave them up to worship the host of heaven" (Acts 7:35–43).
claims.evidence: The NT texts cited (all read as cited verses; the tabernacle/pattern link is Heb 8:5).

claims.claim: The tabernacle and the calf are read typologically in the tradition: the earthly sanctuary prefigures the heavenly (Heb 8–9), Moses' self-offering (32:32) prefigures Paul's (Rom 9:3, per K&D/Bengel), and the veil prefigures a veiled understanding (2 Cor 3:7–18). These are interpretive readings, not the Exodus text's statements.
claims.evidence: Heb 8–9; K&D Ex 32:30–34 (Bengel on Rom 9:3); 2 Cor 3:7–18.

claims.claim: Jeroboam's words at Bethel and Dan — "Behold thy gods, O Israel, which brought thee up out of the land of Egypt" (1 Kgs 12:28) — repeat Ex 32:4 almost verbatim. Many scholars read the calf narrative as a polemic fixing the illegitimacy of the Northern Kingdom's calf cult at the covenant moment (Bible Odyssey); whether Ex 32 was composed as that polemic or Jeroboam's cult is the historical kernel is unresolved.
claims.evidence: KJV 1 Kgs 12:28; Ex 32:4; Bible Odyssey, "The Worship of the Golden Calf".

claims.claim: The canonical order is instructions (25–31) → apostasy (32) → renewal (33–34) → construction (35–40): God gives the pattern of dwelling before Israel proves unworthy of it, and the dwelling is re-granted after the apostasy on the ground of God's Name and Moses' mediation.
claims.evidence: Canonical order of Ex 25–40 (order is observable in the text); the theological point is the dossier's reading — see §3.4.

connections.note: The dwelling promise that opens the instructions (Ex 25:8, "that I may dwell among them") is fulfilled in the promise that closes them ("I will dwell among the children of Israel, and will be their God").
The pattern shown on the mount (Ex 25:9, 40); Hebrews reads the earthly tabernacle as made "according to the pattern shewed to thee in the mount."
The mercy seat as the meeting place (Ex 25:17–22); Leviticus 16:2, 13–15 restricts entry and prescribes the Day of Atonement rite there.

"I will commune with thee from above the mercy seat, from between the two cherubims" (Ex 25:22) — Numbers 7:89 reports Moses hearing the voice speaking "from off the mercy seat… from between the two cherubims."

The seven lamps (Ex 25:31–40); Zechariah's seven-lamp lampstand (4:2) shares the image.

The Urim and the Thummim in the breastplate (Ex 28:30); Deuteronomy 33:8 names the Thummim and Urim as "with thy holy one."

Aaron "bear[s] the iniquity of the holy things" (Ex 28:36–38); Numbers 18:1 assigns the bearing of iniquity to Aaron and the priesthood.

The calf as a visible form of a God who is heard, not seen (Ex 32:5); Deuteronomy 4:12–18 forbids any "similitude" because "ye saw no manner of similitude" (Bible Odyssey's point).

Levi's zeal (Ex 32:26–28, "Who is on the LORD's side?") is formalised in the Levites' appointment (Num 3:5–13).
